item.text: {"text":"Additional uniform negatives can provide broader ranking supervision, but evidence does not establish that increasing their count reliably improves personalized ranking. A SASRec study comparing six samplers across three datasets found uniform sampling favored head items and reinforced popularity bias; popularity-based alternatives sometimes improved balance while reducing aggregate accuracy. Thus, aggregate gains can conceal weaker tail performance ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). False negatives are another plausible mechanism: unobserved items are not confirmed dislikes. UFNRec reports improvements from identifying likely false negatives and applying teacher-generated soft labels, but this does not establish false negatives as the dominant effect of increasing uniform-negative counts ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116)).\n\nSuggested controlled ablation: vary only training-negative count, holding architecture, loss family, temperature, sampling distribution, history exclusions, and seeds fixed; compare both matched optimizer updates and matched GPU time. Keep negative-loss normalization consistent, especially with BCE, where summing additional negatives changes their weight. Report pinned macro validation HR@10 plus per-category and training-frequency head/mid/tail HR@10, recommendation popularity, catalog coverage, duplicate-negative rates, known-positive collisions, and positive–negative score margins. Treat model-based false-negative estimates as proxies, not observed labels. Keep the host’s 99-negative evaluation unchanged: sampled metrics can reverse model ordering relative to full-catalog evaluation, so benchmark gains cannot establish better full-catalog ranking ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/))."}
